name: CertGap — ENERGY STAR vs DOE federal certification cross-audit for appliance brands
one_line: Pre-computed PDF showing an appliance brand, model by model, where its ENERGY STAR listing contradicts its own DOE Compliance Certification Database filing — two federal databases the same manufacturer populated and that are supposed to agree.
buyer: Regulatory Compliance Manager / Director of Product Compliance at appliance manufacturers and importers selling into the US (US entities of brands like Avanti, Danby, Midea, Hisense, Galanz, Element, Curtis International; USA + some UK/EU parent HQs). The person who signs DOE certification reports owns this problem and can card-pay $650 far below any procurement threshold.
source_a: ENERGY STAR certified-product datasets, Socrata open API, no key, no login: https://data.energystar.gov/resource/p5st-her9.json (residential refrigerators), q8py-6w3f.json (dishwashers), bghd-e2wd.json (clothes washers). ~60 product categories available.
source_b: DOE Compliance Certification Database (CCMS) public Solr endpoint, no login: POST https://www.regulations.doe.gov/certification-data/solr/ccms/select (discovered via the site's own JS; per-product-group fq, wildcard rows, faceting all work). Covers ~70 federally regulated product groups.
the_defect: "ENERGY STAR's federal database lists your washer WF5S2845BW at IMEF 2.92. Your own DOE certification on file (regulations.doe.gov) shows 1.84 for the same model number. One of your two federal filings is wrong — and DOE fined 35 companies for certification failures in 2023 alone." Real fetched examples: Avanti AV1081VFK0W fridge 249 kWh/yr (ENERGY STAR) vs 354 kWh/yr (DOE); Bosch SHX78DC** dishwasher 215 vs 240 kWh/yr; Maytag MHW5630M** IMEF 2.92 vs 2.76.
fetch_proof: ALL FETCHED THIS SESSION. ENERGY STAR: HTTP 200, refrigerators 4,748 rows / dishwashers 748 / clothes washers 394, with brand, model number, kWh-yr, IMEF fields. DOE Solr: HTTP 200, numFound=14,021 refrigerator-freezer records / 1,537 dishwashers / 1,763 washers; full-database facet query returned 4,595,423 total certification records and 7,227 distinct brand names. Join I actually ran (model-number match incl. wildcard handling): 3,001 ENERGY STAR models matched into DOE across the 3 categories; 159 disagree on the certified energy figure = 5.3% mismatch (5.3% fridges, 5.4% dishwashers, 5.4% washers — stable across categories). 44 of 169 matched brands carry >=1 mismatch. ADV-Check's W3 (unmeasured mismatch rate) is answered here with a measured 5.3%.
list_size: 7,227 distinct brand names counted by Solr facet across all 70 DOE product groups (brands roll up to fewer owning companies, realistically 2,000-4,000 [UNKNOWN exact]); 169 brands enumerated in my 3-category join, 44 already holding a named, quotable defect. Smaller universe than ADV's 15k firms, but every prospect is pre-qualified by a computed defect before contact.
repeat: Quarterly monitoring subscription per brand: DOE updates the CCD roughly biweekly, ENERGY STAR lists new models continuously (date_qualified shows constant flow), brands launch SKUs monthly and span many product groups (Midea/Hisense sell in 15+ categories). Same customer re-buys per quarter and per category — vs ADV-Check's once-a-year cycle. Also cross-sell: 'ES model absent from DOE entirely' (the exact violation behind most 2023 DOE penalties) and FTC EnergyGuide label checks give multiple findings per customer so the free email sample never exhausts the product.
delivery: Pre-computed PDF report per brand (defect table with side-by-side quoted values, public URLs to both federal records, screenshots), regenerated quarterly. Buyer installs nothing, needs no AI account.
weakest_link: Some fraction of the 5.3% may be benign version skew (one database updated before the other) or wildcard-model-number artifacts rather than true miscertification — if a compliance manager can wave off the sample as 'databases lag', reply rates collapse. Mitigation is to lead only with large persistent deltas (e.g. 249 vs 354 kWh). Second risk: at giant brands (Whirlpool, LG, Bosch) the finding routes to legal instead of a card.
evidence: [VERIFIED] data.energystar.gov Socrata API open, no key: p5st-her9 (4,748 rows), q8py-6w3f (748), bghd-e2wd (394) — fetched HTTP 200. [VERIFIED] DOE CCMS Solr endpoint https://www.regulations.doe.gov/certification-data/solr/ccms/select open (needs browser User-Agent header): 14,021/1,537/1,763 rows per category, 4,595,423 records and 7,227 brands database-wide — fetched HTTP 200. [VERIFIED] Computed join: 3,001 matched models, 159 mismatches (5.3%), 44 brands affected, named examples incl. Bosch, Maytag, LG, Hisense, Avanti, Danby. [PLAUSIBLE] DOE enforcement escalation and penalties up to $560/unit or per-day for certification failures; 46 EPCA settlements in 2023, 35 for certification violations — law-firm alert https://www.crowell.com/en/insights/client-alerts/appliance-standards-steep-increase-in-department-of-energy-enforcement-cases-puts-appliance-manufacturers-and-importers-at-financial-risk and DOE civil-penalty policy PDF (search-sourced, not independently parsed). [VERIFIED-BY-ABSENCE, searched] No incumbent product doing ES-vs-DOE database consistency audits found; DOE's own site disclaims data accuracy and publishes no cross-validator; EPA verification tests physical units, not database consistency.

name: 990 Integrity Report — a nonprofit's own consecutive IRS filings that contradict each other
one_line: Pre-computed report flagging where a nonprofit's latest Form 990 contradicts its own prior-year 990 (prior-year revenue column and net-asset roll-forward that don't tie) — the exact inconsistencies grantmakers and auditors trip over.
buyer: CFO / finance director of mid-size US nonprofits ($1M-$50M revenue), or the small CPA firms preparing their 990s; USA.
source_a: IRS TEOS 990 e-file bulk data, free, no login: index https://apps.irs.gov/pub/epostcard/990/xml/2025/index_2025.csv and full XML zips (e.g. 2025_TEOS_XML_01A.zip).
source_b: The same organization's prior-year Form 990 — also public IRS data (cross-checked this session via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer API, https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/api/v2/organizations/{ein}.json, free, no key).
the_defect: "Your FY2023 Form 990 Part I reports prior-year total revenue of $980,839. The FY2022 Form 990 you actually filed reports $966,836. The two filings differ by $14,003 with no restatement note — any grantmaker comparing them sees the same gap." (Real fetched example: EIN 364478169.)
fetch_proof: ALL FETCHED THIS SESSION. index_2025.csv: HTTP 200, 93MB, 748,906 return rows, of which 376,920 are full Form 990s. Batch 2025_TEOS_XML_01A.zip: HTTP 200, 103MB, 17,044 XML returns, parsed. Measured on random samples of 60 consecutive-year org pairs each: prior-year-revenue-column mismatch 1/60 (1.7%); net-asset roll-forward (BOY vs prior EOY) mismatch 1/60 (1.7%). ProPublica API HTTP 200 throughout.
list_size: 376,920 organizations filing full Form 990 counted in the 2025 index alone (748,906 returns all types) — 25x ADV-Check's universe. But at the measured ~1.7% per defect class, pre-qualified prospects are roughly 6,000-13,000/yr.
repeat: Annual at best — one 990 per year, same structural weakness as ADV-Check's W1. No honest quarterly angle.
delivery: Pre-computed PDF citing both public filings with page/line references.
weakest_link: I measured it and it is weak: only 1.7% incidence per defect class (vs 5.3% for CertGap), the dollar consequence of a $14k prior-year discrepancy is mild embarrassment rather than regulator risk, and nonprofits are poor card-buyers at any price above ~$250. Data says this is a backup only if more defect classes (Schedule cross-foots, state-filing comparisons) push combined incidence past ~10% — unproven.
evidence: [VERIFIED] IRS index fetched: 748,906 rows / 376,920 Form 990s (HTTP 200). [VERIFIED] 103MB XML batch fetched and parsed: 17,044 returns (HTTP 200). [VERIFIED] Measured mismatch rates on 120 sampled consecutive-year pairs: 1.7% prior-year revenue column, 1.7% net-asset roll-forward, with named example EIN 364478169 ($980,839 vs $966,836). [VERIFIED] ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer API open and free. [UNKNOWN] Whether additional defect classes raise incidence enough to sustain outreach economics; nonprofit willingness-to-pay at $250 untested.

name: PublicFile Guard - quarterly FCC public-inspection-file audit for radio stations
one_line: Pre-computed PDF audit telling a named radio station owner exactly which FCC-required Quarterly Issues/Programs Lists are missing or time-stamped late in their own FCC-hosted public file, re-sold every quarter as a monitoring report ahead of the 2027-2030 license-renewal certification.
buyer: Owner / General Manager / Market Manager of a small-to-mid US radio group (1-30 stations), USA. Small-market owners routinely pay by card; no procurement.
source_a: FCC LMS facility database dump (free, no login): https://enterpriseefiling.fcc.gov/dataentry/api/download/dbfile/08-06-2026/facility.zip - enumerates every licensed station with facility_id, callsign, community, license status.
source_b: FCC Online Public Inspection File API (free, no key): https://publicfiles.fcc.gov/api/manager/folder/id/{folderId}.json?entityId={facilityId} - returns every file in the station's own 'Issues and Programs Lists' folder WITH FCC-stamped create_ts upload timestamps; folder IDs scraped from https://publicfiles.fcc.gov/fm-profile/{callsign}/more-public-files.
the_defect: "Your station WCXL's FCC public file (link) contains no Issues/Programs list for 2024Q3, 2024Q4, 2025Q1 or 2025Q2, and KVNF's 2025Q1 list carries the FCC's own upload stamp of 2025-12-01 - 235 days after the April 10 deadline in 47 CFR 73.3526(e)(12). Your 2027-2030 renewal application requires certifying these were placed on time; missing lists were the largest source of $10,000-$15,000 renewal fines last cycle." Every fact is on the FCC's own page about their own station.
fetch_proof: All fetched by me today: (1) facility.zip HTTP 200, 10,083,293 bytes, 180,816 rows; I counted 11,161 licensed full-power FM + 4,874 full-power AM + 918 TV by callsign/frequency classification. (2) Folder API HTTP 200 per station, e.g. WNYC-FM entityId 73355 returned its full Issues/Programs file list with timestamps (one file named '2014Q2' stamped uploaded 2022-01-21). (3) I ran a live audit of 30 randomly sampled full-power FMs: 11/30 had >=1 quarter with no matching list since 2024 (e.g. KBHU-FM and KDRX: zero lists in 9 quarters; KMSL: nothing since 2019), 6/30 more were only late (e.g. WZFL 2024Q1 uploaded 791 days late; KORL-FM 2025Q4 180 days late) - 17/30 (57%) defective, excluding the shutdown-affected 2025Q3 from all counts. (4) Enforcement primary source: DA-26-434A1.pdf fetched from docs.fcc.gov, HTTP 200, 121,180 bytes - WABG(AM) renewal held to a public-file consent decree with civil penalty.
list_size: 16,035 licensed full-power radio stations (11,161 FM + 4,874 AM) counted by me from the fetched facility.dat, plus ~1,700 full-power/Class A TV - roughly 17,700 stations, several thousand distinct owners/groups. [VERIFIED by my own parse of facility.zip]
repeat: Quarterly by construction: a new list is due Jan/Apr/Jul/Oct 10 every quarter forever, so the same owner buys a $250-350 per-quarter verification report per group (initial gap audit $450-500). The 57% measured defect rate shows stations do NOT self-check. ~90 recurring group customers at $350/quarter covers the R$30k/month target ($8.4k/mo); with 3,000+ multi-station owners in the list that is <3% penetration. Renewal-cycle fear (radio renewals restart June 2027) drives the initial purchase; the subscription is 'never fail a certification again'.
delivery: Pre-computed PDF per group: per-station grid of all 32 renewal-cycle quarters, marked present / MISSING / late (with the FCC's own timestamp), direct links to each empty folder, plus a one-page fix checklist and the renewal-certification language it protects. Nothing to install; buyer verifies every line by clicking their own public-file URL.
weakest_link: The fix is trivial (upload a Word doc), so once alerted a group's staff can DIY the go-forward checking with a calendar reminder - monitoring churn risk pushes the quarterly price toward $250. Secondary risks: FCC sent its own mass warning letters once (2019) and could again; and ~a third of my 'missing' flags could be exotic file-naming my matcher missed (I found and fixed two such false negatives, KFCF and KDUV, during sampling - true miss rate is more like 40% than 57%). Broadcast lawyers publish free deadline advisories, but nobody sells the automated named-station gap detection. [Competitor scan: only law-firm advisories and syndicated-content vendors like MediaTracks surfaced; sources: pillsburylaw.com, broadcastlawblog.com, commlawcenter.com, mediatracks.com]
evidence: [VERIFIED] facility.zip fetch+count (URL above, 200, 180,816 rows). [VERIFIED] OPIF folder API with timestamps for WNYC-FM 73355 and 42 sampled stations (URLs above, all 200). [VERIFIED] 30-station random audit results as listed in fetch_proof. [VERIFIED] docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-434A1.pdf (renewal consent decree, civil penalty). [PLAUSIBLE] $10k-$15k typical fines for missing lists at renewal and $25k-$29k recent consent decrees - pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/2026-second-quarter-issues-programs-list-advisory-broadcast-stations.html, commlawcenter.com/2026/05/fcc-enforcement-monitor-may-2026.html, broadcastlawblog.com 2019 warning-letter post. [PLAUSIBLE] 2025Q3 deadline extension due to government shutdown (inferred from the Nov 18-20 2025 upload cluster across 5 independent stations in my sample + broadcastlawblog shutdown post); I excluded that quarter from all defect counts. [UNKNOWN] exact count of distinct owners; deducible from LMS ownership tables (same free dump family).

name: LDA Reconcile - quarterly LD-2 vs LD-203 gap report for federal lobbying firms
one_line: Pre-computed reconciliation showing a named lobbying firm which of the lobbyists listed on its own quarterly LD-2 reports never filed the semiannual LD-203 contribution report the Senate's database says is due - sold per filing cycle, 4-6 times a year.
buyer: Principal or office manager at a small/boutique federal lobbying firm (2-20 lobbyists), Washington DC, USA. Firm principal holds the card; no committee.
source_a: Senate LDA REST API - LD-2 quarterly activity filings naming each active lobbyist: https://lda.senate.gov/api/v1/filings/?filing_year=2025&filing_period=fourth_quarter&filing_type=Q4 (free, no key, anonymous).
source_b: Same authority's LD-203 contribution-report index, which must contain one entry per named lobbyist per half-year: https://lda.senate.gov/api/v1/contributions/?registrant_id={id}&filing_year=2025&filing_period=year_end (free, no key).
the_defect: "Your Q4-2025 LD-2 for the International Association of Chiefs of Police lists Eugene Voegtlin as an active lobbyist. The Senate's contribution database shows no year-end 2025 LD-203 for him (due January 30, 2026) - search his name yourself at lda.senate.gov. Each missing LD-203 is referrable to the U.S. Attorney with civil penalties up to $200,000." Two records in the buyer's own regulator's database that must cross-reference and don't.
fetch_proof: All fetched by me today, anonymous, no key: registrants endpoint 200 (count 17,440); LD-2 filings Q1-2026 count 21,804, Q4-2025 count 20,940; LD-203 contributions 2026 count 16,822. Live cross-check of 20 registrants from Q4-2025 LD-2s: 6 of 33 named lobbyists (18%) had no year-end-2025 LD-203 under their firm; global dedupe by lobbyist_id then CONFIRMED Eugene Voegtlin (id 46300) filed nothing anywhere (count 0) and EXPOSED one false positive (David Vitter filed under a different firm-scoped id, count 1) - honest post-dedupe gap rate ~10-15% of lobbyists, touching roughly 1 in 4-5 firms.
list_size: 17,440 registrants in the Senate API (my fetch, count field); ~21,000 LD-2 filings per quarter implies several thousand currently-active registrant firms; every filing carries the firm's address and contact/posted-by name for outreach. [VERIFIED counts; distinct-active-registrant count not yet computed]
repeat: Built-in calendar: LD-2 due Jan/Apr/Jul/Oct 20, LD-203 due Jan 30 and Jul 30 - 4-6 reconciliation events per firm per year, sold at $300 per cycle or $250/quarter standing order. ~28 recurring firms at $300/cycle x 4.5 cycles covers the $8k/month target; the active-registrant pool is in the thousands, so the acquisition treadmill stops early if repeat holds.
delivery: Pre-computed PDF per firm per cycle: roster of every lobbyist named on the firm's own LD-2s, matched line-by-line against LD-203 records, with the exact Senate search URL for each gap, plus late-filing timestamps (dt_posted vs statutory deadline) and terminated-lobbyist loose ends. Nothing to install.
weakest_link: The authority notifies eventually: the Secretary of the Senate/Clerk send their own noncompliance letters and refer to the US Attorney, and real-world penalty enforcement is famously lax - so the fear is 'embarrassing referral letter', not existential, capping price near $250-300. Second: person-matching across the API's registrant-scoped lobbyist IDs means every flagged gap needs a name-level dedupe (my sample had 1 confirmed false positive in 6 flags), so reports must show only globally-confirmed gaps. Big law/compliance shops (Wiley, Venable) sell manual LDA compliance services to larger firms, though no automated per-firm gap report surfaced. [Sources: venable.com LDA overview PDF, wiley.law lobbying-and-campaign-finance-reporting, lobbyingdisclosure.house.gov]
evidence: [VERIFIED] lda.senate.gov/api/v1/registrants/ (200, count 17,440); /filings/ Q1-2026 count 21,804 and Q4-2025 count 20,940; /contributions/ 2026 count 16,822; BGR Government Affairs year-end-2025 LD-203 set (51 records, all lobbyist-type, dt_posted 2026-01-30); Voegtlin lobbyist_id 46300 year-end-2025 contributions count 0 (genuine gap); Vitter id 68761 count 1 (false positive caught). All fetched anonymously today. [VERIFIED] filer_type query param is ignored by the API - registrant-level (firm's own) LD-203 checking needs a different query and was excluded from my measured rates. [PLAUSIBLE] $200k statutory max civil penalty and semiannual Jan 30/Jul 30 deadlines - venable.com/-/media/files/publications/2025/03/federal-lobbying-disclosure-act.pdf and lobbyingdisclosure.house.gov. [PLAUSIBLE] GAO annual audits find ~10% of lobbyists non-compliant with LD-203, consistent with my measured 18% pre-dedupe / ~10-15% post-dedupe.

name: RangeGap - Pay Transparency Posting Exposure Report
one_line: Pre-computed PDF showing a named employer every live job ad of theirs that omits the salary range now required in NY/CA/CO/WA/IL etc., found by scanning their own public ATS feed before contact, re-sold as a monthly/quarterly re-scan because postings churn.
buyer: Head of Talent Acquisition / HR Director at US mid-market company (50-1,000 employees) hiring in pay-transparency states, USA
source_a: The company's own live job ads via free public ATS JSON: https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{slug}/jobs?content=true and https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{slug}?mode=json (no auth, no key)
source_b: The same posting's own location field + the ATS pay_input_ranges field (https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{slug}/jobs/{id}?pay_transparency=true) - a covered-jurisdiction location with an empty range field is a missing-required-field defect (D3 'missing required field' class, not a two-document contradiction; the statute is the second 'source')
the_defect: "Your live posting 'Head Preschool Teacher (2-Year-Olds)' (job-boards.greenhouse.io/vivvi/jobs/7595127003) is for New York City and displays no compensation range - NYC Local Law 32 / NY Labor Law 194-b require one in the ad itself. Three more of your current ads have the same gap; page 2 lists them. Washington's amended EPOA gives a 5-business-day cure window after notice." [VERIFIED: I fetched that job and 10 others; all render with pay_input_ranges=[] and no $ figure in the ad body]
fetch_proof: All fetched today: (1) boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/stripe/jobs?content=true HTTP 200, 4.2MB, 552 jobs; (2) Wayback CDX (web.archive.org/cdx) paged with resumeKey: ~1.1M archived URLs parsed -> 12,301 unique Greenhouse board slugs + 3,313 unique Lever slugs (2023+); Common Crawl index 504'd, Wayback worked; (3) live sample of 50 random Greenhouse slugs: 20 live (HTTP 200 with jobs), 30 dead; 36 covered-state postings checked, 11 had no $ range in ad content, and 11/11 confirmed pay_input_ranges=[] via the per-job endpoint - real companies flagged: Vivvi (4 NYC childcare ads), Talkspace Psychiatry (CA/CO/IL/DC remote NP roles), Dotmatics (Remote-USA AE); (4) Lever verified live: api.lever.co/v0/postings/palantir HTTP 200, 301 postings; /spotify 200, 106 postings; (5) false-positive check: Stripe NYC job 7993151 has empty API pay_input_ranges BUT its self-hosted page stripe.com/jobs/listing/... renders '$312,000 - $468,000' - so self-hosted career pages need a page fetch, Greenhouse-hosted pages (the majority of SMB/mid-market) are safe to judge from the API alone
list_size: 15,614 named-company ATS boards enumerated free (12,301 Greenhouse + 3,313 Lever unique slugs, counted by parsing ~1.1M Wayback CDX URLs) [VERIFIED]; live-rate sample 20/50 implies roughly 5,000-6,500 currently-live Greenhouse boards [VERIFIED sample, extrapolation mine]; Ashby/Workable/SmartRecruiters extend it further [UNKNOWN]. In the live sample, 3 of 20 boards (15%) carried a confirmed defect even with only 25 jobs/board and a narrow location regex - pre-qualified prospect yield is high
repeat: High - this is its main edge over ADV-Check. Job postings churn weekly; every new requisition is a new exposure; new state laws keep taking effect (IL/MN/NJ 2025, MA/VT phasing in); WA's 2025 amendment (SB 5408, verified via Ogletree/Morgan Lewis alerts) created a 5-business-day cure window through July 2027, which makes EARLY detection concretely valuable and justifies a standing monthly/quarterly re-scan of the same customer at the same price
delivery: Pre-computed PDF: every flagged posting with its URL, screenshot, the jurisdiction trigger (location string), and a compliant-range checklist; recurring customers get the same PDF re-generated monthly. Buyer installs nothing
weakest_link: The consequence layer ('this violates NYC LL32') is a legal claim, which edges toward borrowed authority - mitigated because pay-transparency laws are now common HR knowledge and the missing range itself is verifiable in 10 seconds on the buyer's own ad, but a lawyer-averse HR lead may forward the email to counsel instead of paying a stranger $497. Second risk: enterprise comp platforms (Syndio-class) already ship ATS-integrated 'posting audit' features [PLAUSIBLE, compensationtools.net roundup] - not sold standalone to mid-market from outside, but the category could commoditize. Third: buyer can silently fix the 4 named ads for free; the paid product must be the FULL sweep + monitoring, not the sample
evidence: Strongest verified facts: free no-auth enumeration of 15,614 named employers' live ads; 31% of covered-state postings in a random sample (11/36) lacked ranges with pay_input_ranges=[] confirmed per-job; named real defects at Vivvi, Talkspace Psychiatry, Dotmatics fetched today; WA statutory damages $100-$5,000 per violation with private right of action and a cure window [VERIFIED via L&I/law-firm alerts: lni.wa.gov, ogletree.com, morganlewis.com]; NYC penalties up to $250,000 [PLAUSIBLE, widely reported]. Honest caveat: no head-to-head competitor scan found selling this outside-in to mid-market, but absence is [UNKNOWN], not proven

name: Provider Record Consistency Report (NPPES vs CMS Care Compare vs own website)
one_line: Quarterly pre-computed report for a medical group practice listing, clinician by clinician, where the two federal databases payers actually pull from (NPPES and CMS Doctors & Clinicians) disagree with each other and with the group's own website - addresses, phones, affiliations, decade-stale records.
buyer: Practice administrator / office manager at a US medical group practice of 5-50 clinicians, USA
source_a: NPPES NPI Registry public API, free, no key: https://npiregistry.cms.hhs.gov/api/?version=2.1&number={npi} [VERIFIED HTTP 200 today]
source_b: CMS Doctors & Clinicians National Downloadable File (DAC), free datastore API: https://data.cms.gov/provider-data/api/1/datastore/query/mj5m-pzi6/0 [VERIFIED HTTP 200, count=3,387,942 rows, modified 2026-06-26]; third leg = the group's own website roster
the_defect: "NPPES record 1184203739 lists Dr. Capelli's practice phone as 570-808-7850; Medicare Care Compare lists 570-826-7300 for the same clinician at the same address - two federal databases your payers pull from disagree. Dr. Verespy's NPPES record still shows 177 Fort Washington Ave, New York (her prior employer) though she bills from your address. One clinician's NPPES record was last updated in 2012." [VERIFIED - all three examples fetched live today]
fetch_proof: Fetched today: DAC metadata + row count via datastore API (HTTP 200, 3,387,942 rows, columns incl. npi, org_pac_id, num_org_mem, address, telephone_number); pulled 20 distinct NPIs from DAC and queried each against NPPES API (20 HTTP 200s): naive compare gave 20/20 mismatching on address-or-phone; manually confirmed the phone conflict is real, not a parsing artifact (NPPES 570-808-7850 vs DAC 570-826-7300 for NPI 1184203739) and found genuinely stale records (NPPES last_updated 2012-02-09; an NPPES address pointing at a prior NY employer)
list_size: 3,387,942 clinician-location rows in DAC [VERIFIED via count=true on the datastore API]; distinct group practices not separately counted - the API's group-by did not reduce the count and I did not page the full file, so distinct-org total is [UNKNOWN], plausibly low hundreds of thousands given num_org_mem distribution; either way the named, addressable universe dwarfs ADV-Check's 15k
repeat: Quarterly by design: CAQH requires provider re-attestation roughly every 120 days and No Surprises Act rules push plans to re-verify directory data every 90 days [PLAUSIBLE - caqh.org issue brief and vendor literature, not fetched as primary rule text], so the same practice has a standing calendar reason to re-buy the refreshed report every quarter
delivery: Pre-computed PDF per practice: one row per clinician x data element (address, phone, specialty, affiliation) across NPPES / Care Compare / own website, mismatches highlighted, with the exact free portal (NPPES, PECOS, CAQH) where each fix is made. Buyer installs nothing
weakest_link: The defect is AMBIENT, not scarce - my naive sample mismatched 20/20 (partly noise: 'BLVD' vs 'DR', multi-location clinicians), so 'your records disagree' may read as 'everyone's do' and lose its sting; the report must curate hard (different city, dead phone, decade-stale) to stay alarming. Also the fixes are free self-service portals, and credentialing-maintenance vendors (Neolytix-class, $99-199/provider/yr territory [PLAUSIBLE]) already sell adjacent upkeep to this exact buyer, which is real T3 pressure - this candidate is honestly weaker than RangeGap on differentiation, stronger on recurrence-by-calendar
evidence: Verified core: both federal sources free, no-auth, bulk-queryable; real cross-source contradictions fetched live (conflicting phones in NPPES vs DAC for the same NPI at the same address; NPPES address at a clinician's prior employer; a 2012-stale record); DAC refreshed 2026-06-26 so the comparison is against current data. Market context [PLAUSIBLE]: CAQH/ASPE literature documents chronic directory inaccuracy and existing vendors serve health PLANS at enterprise scale, not 5-50-clinician groups from outside
